https://www.autoexpress.co.uk/dacia/3659.text: News Home Dacia New Dacia Spring confirmed for September reveal and super low price The new Spring will be based on the adorable Renault Twingo and built here in Europe By: Ellis Hyde 22 Jul 2026 7 The new Dacia Spring will be unveiled in September, Auto Express can confirm. The next iteration of the brand’s no-nonsense, cut-price electric car will continue to focus on the simple bare necessities of motoring. The current Spring may have only arrived in the UK two years ago, but it was launched in Europe back in 2021 so it’s about time for an all-new replacement. More than 200,000 examples have been sold across Europe since the city car hit the streets, explaining why its successor will carry forward the Spring name. Cheapest electric cars on sale 2026 Supposedly the new Dacia Spring has been developed in just 16 months. This is even faster than the Renault Twingo it’s based upon that went from green light to production in 21 months – an unprecedented feat for a European carmaker. Advertisement - Article continues below In an exclusive interview with Auto Express, Dacia CEO Katrin Adt reaffirmed the goal is to have the new Dacia Spring start from less than 18,000 euros (around £15,000 at the current exchange rate) and the car’s rapid-fire development has helped achieve this. But she added, “I also think the most important thing is that we have, again, used our Dacia DNA to design it to cost and to really reduce everything to the essential. Skip advert Advertisement Skip advert Advertisement - Article continues below “Therefore, this car has strictly what the customer needs, and nothing else. It’s amazing to see that Dacia is capable of doing that in any segment.” Adt was a 10-year veteran of Mercedes-Benz before taking on the top job at Dacia, and the two companies have very different philosophies. “Coming from Mercedes, I only knew engineers who are packing things in the car. While in Romania, we have a team of engineers who are taking things out of the car, which is fascinating to see. “I was very much in favor of that and it is also a definite proof of how consistent this brand is. So there is our brand value, essential and cool, and you see that in everything we are doing.” What will the new Dacia city car look like? 7 As we said, the new Dacia Spring will be the more pragmatic sister car to the irresistible Renault Twingo , but rather than a bubbly city car, the Dacia is going to be a sub-four-metre SUV with rather chunky proportions. Despite the car’s diminutive size, Dacia even promises the cut-price EV will have seating for four people and a “proper boot”. Advertisement - Article continues below Looking at the prototypes in our spy images, it’s clear that this car will share its fundamental structure with the Twingo, but Dacia’s design boss David Durand assured us he and his team have enough freedom to create something uniquely Dacia. Skip advert Advertisement Skip advert Advertisement - Article continues below “I’m sure you will recognise it as a real Dacia. It was important to differentiate completely [new Spring] from Renault and not have a similar offering with the two brands. It would make no sense because we will start to compete and this is not at all what we want to do.” The designers have been able to separate the two visually by using plenty of clever tricks. The first is the Dacia’s taller and more defined bonnet, which gives it a more conventional two-box silhouette. Beneath the new bonnet are a pair of boxy LED headlights that’ll probably be joined by a large grille-like graphic as seen on other Dacia models. However, while the nose will be quite different in design, the side windows look to be carried straight over from the Renault, including the pop-out openings for the rear glass. At the back, expect similarly high placements for the rear lights, but these will be squarer and more conventional in design than the Twingo’s clever LED hoops. Advertisement - Article continues below Inside, we expect the pair to share their dashboard layout and general design, however Dacia will utilise its less colourful palette of recycled materials. The digital interfaces are also to be shared and should include a digital driver’s display paired with a Google-based 10-inch touchscreen. One of the Twingo’s iconic elements, the movable twin rear seats, could be reverted to a more traditional bench in order to help keep a cap on the Dacia’s costs. What battery and motors will be fitted? 7 As well as the shared basic structure, Dacia’s plan to keep costs low will include the direct carry-over of the Twingo’s electric motor and battery layout. This means we’re expecting to see a 27.5kWh battery pack combined with an 80bhp electric motor mounted on the front axle. It’s far too early to be specific about range or performance, but it should broadly match the Twingo’s 163-mile electric range, and 50kW DC charging speed. Skip advert Advertisement Skip advert Advertisement - Article continues below The Dacia will have a longer range and better charging capabilities than the entry-level BYD Dolphin Surf , while also substantially undercutting it in price. This also means it’ll usurp the old Spring considerably, however the Leapmotor T03 will still probably offer more range for your buck with 175 miles at around £16,000. Advertisement - Article continues below As with the Twingo, this Dacia has had a fast-tracked development that will bring it to market very quickly, but it will also mean we’ll have to wait a little longer than our friends in continental Europe for it to arrive. Right-hand drive production of the Twingo doesn’t commence until the beginning of 2027, so expect the Dacia to follow after that date, even if we see the completed car in the next few months. How much will the new Dacia Spring cost? We’re not expecting it to arrive in the UK until 2027, but when it does, prices could start from as low as £15,000, ensuring it retains the title of the UK’s cheapest electric car that the current model has held since coming here. Patrice Lévy-Bencheton, Dacia’s VP for product performance hinted as much when Auto Express spoke to him about the new Spring: “We do essential cars; we do only what the customer really needs. Skip advert Advertisement Skip advert Advertisement - Article continues below “We define our product according to what we get from the customer survey, what insights we get in terms of real needs and real usages. And this is, for us, the better way to stay where we are on the market; position [the new Spring] as the most affordable EV on the market by far. You can count on us to continue to defend, let's say, this position on the market”. We don’t expect the old and new Spring will be in showrooms together, but the current model has recently been updated so it can hang on until its successor arrives. Importantly, however, the new one will be made in Europe, whereas the outgoing model is built in China and at the mercy of European tariffs that could raise its price by as much as 35 per cent. Why build a second small EV at all? 7 Speaking on the media call discussing Dacia’s 2025 H1 financial results, Frank Marotte told Auto Express: “[Dacia is] committed to increasing our BEV share, our BEV volumes, and our contribution to the Renault Group’s CAFE (Corporate Average Fuel Economy). “So we keep developing the model that was announced earlier this year by (ex-Renault CEO) Luca de Meo, and we will bring more news to you in the coming months about this. You will not wait for too long,” Marotte told us. The existing Dacia Spring is one of the very cheapest EVs money can buy. However, you could save even more via the Auto Express Buy a Car service ... https://www.politico.eu/article/poland-s.text: Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski on Wednesday threatened to reconsider Warsaw’s $50 million-a-year spending on Elon Musk’s Starlink network, joining a growing government backlash over new roaming restrictions set to hit Polish customers later this month. “Hey, @elonmusk, big man, stop discriminating Polish users of Starlink or we might re-think paying you $50 million p.a. for your services,” wrote Sikorski on X. The foreign minister's anger follows Starlink’s decision to exclude Poland from a shared European roaming zone that covers more than 30 countries, including Germany, Czechia, Slovakia and Lithuania. Customers within the zone can take their terminals across borders without triggering international-use restrictions. But Polish users will now face extra requirements when traveling. Advertisement Advertisement “Note: Poland is not included in the Europe region above. Accounts registered in Poland are treated as Poland-only for home-country use,” reads Starlink’s current guidance . Polish Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski also went after Musk, accusing Starlink's parent company SpaceX of treating Poles as second-class customers and demanding it spell out the regulatory basis for the change. “Poland is not a second-tier market. Polish customers are not second-tier customers,” Gawkowski wrote on X. If SpaceX blames “local regulatory requirements,” Warsaw expects it to point to the specific rules rather than offer “general explanations,” he added. The new rules have applied to new customers signing up for Starlink since July 14, 2026 and will extend to existing Polish users on Aug. 17. This isn't the first time Sikorski and Musk have fought over Starlink. Last year, Musk told the Polish minister to “be quiet, small man,” after Sikorski warned that Warsaw could seek alternative providers for the satellite service it's financing for Ukraine. SpaceX did not immediately respond to POLITICO's request for comment. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text: Cars are becoming ‘increasingly smart’ with digital systems that collect data and connect to the internet, the General Intelligence and Security Service said. Photograph: Tamer Adel/Alamy View image in fullscreen Cars are becoming ‘increasingly smart’ with digital systems that collect data and connect to the internet, the General Intelligence and Security Service said. Photograph: Tamer Adel/Alamy Motoring Tech in cars can be used to snoop on you, Dutch spy chiefs warn Hostile states could access cameras, microphones or GPS, says intelligence agency amid concerns over Chinese imports Alex Daniel Thu 1 Oct 2026 06.49 EDT First published on Thu 1 Oct 2026 06.25 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Drivers have been warned that the smart features built into modern cars such as microphones, cameras and GPS trackers could be used by hostile states to spy on them. The Dutch General Intelligence and Security Service (AIVD) called for “awareness of espionage risks around modern vehicles”, including microphones that can by switched on remotely to listen to conversations. It did not mention an individual country, but the warning will add to concerns around a recent boom in Chinese car imports into the UK. Three-quarters of UK’s popular plug-in hybrid cars unable to use rapid chargers Read more In a translated document released on Wednesday, the AIVD said cars were becoming “increasingly smart” with digital systems that collected data and connected to the internet. “On the one hand this offers practical benefits, but on the other hand these systems collect a great deal of data about occupants, the vehicle itself, and about objects and people in the vicinity. Various parties, including state actors, can gain access to this data,” it added. The alert follows reports last year that British defence firms working for the UK government had cautioned staff against connecting or pairing their phones with Chinese-made electric cars, owing to fears that Beijing could extract sensitive data from the devices. Chinese-owned brands now account for 15% of all new cars registered in the UK, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, almost 175,000 vehicles in the first half of 2026 and more than double the same period last year. Models by MG, BYD and Jaecoo, whose parent company Chery is part-owned by the Chinese state, have led the surge, popular for their low price and in-car technology. The Jaecoo 7 was the UK’s bestselling car in March. MPs have raised concerns that China’s national intelligence law requires its companies to assist the state’s intelligence services when requested. The UK Ministry of Defence has said it is working with other government departments “to understand and mitigate any potential threats to national security” from vehicles. This year, the MoD reportedly banned cars with Chinese parts from sensitive military sites, including RAF Wyton in Cambridgeshire and the Dorset headquarters of Britain’s maritime special forces, the SBS. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion The AIVD said it was “technically possible to activate” microphones and cameras remotely in some cars, allowing malicious actors to “eavesdrop on conversations” and “make recordings in and around the vehicle”. The agency added that drivers should “not hold confidential conversations in or around the vehicle”, or “use a vehicle with an external camera when travelling to a sensitive location”. It also said connecting phones and other devices, either via Bluetooth, wifi or charging systems could allow malicious actors to “extract data from connected devices via the vehicle”. The AIVD suggested systems such as GPS navigation systems, telematics modules and charging stations could all be used to gather and send data about the car and drivers’ whereabouts elsewhere. On Wednesday, MI5 issued a rare public warning to UK universities to stop working with the China General Technology Research Institute, which it said was being used as a front by Beijing’s intelligence service to pay for research by UK academics and steal the secrets of hi-tech projects. The Chinese embassy in London issued a strongly worded rebuttal, describing the accusations as “imaginary and purely fabricated”. Subscribe to LBC Catch Up Plus from Â£4.99 a month By Chay Quinn A plan to see the NHS in England deliver "world-class cancer care" is being delayed, diluted and underfunded, according to experts. It comes after health officials made a correction to the National Cancer Plan which alters a pledge made in the original document. The plan, published in February, said that the Government will pay Â£70 million for 28 new radiotherapy machines which would lead to 27,500 more patients to receive treatment each year. But officials made a correction to the document, highlighting how this investment will lead to 27,500 more âtreatmentsâ annually. Experts said that radiotherapy is delivered over a course of treatments, which can be anywhere between five and 25 sessions depending on the type of cancer and treatment plan. They said this means fewer patients will receive treatment than originally suggested. Professor Pat Price, from Imperial College London and chair of Radiotherapy UK, said: âCancer care needs real authority to deliver the right change and a clear line of accountability if we are going to turn this crisis around. âThe correction to the cancer plan shows exactly why conflating patients with treatments is not a trivial mistake; it can dramatically overstate how many people new treatments will help and lead to dangerous underinvestment. âAnd this goes beyond one error. Frontline clinicians are telling us that across the country the changes radiotherapy cancer treatments need are simply not happening, and local planning for new machines and treatment centres can feel almost non-existent.â An analysis by cancer experts, published in The Lancet Oncology, says that ministers âmake national promises but do not have the levers to ensure deliveryâ. âThis situation is a disaster for patients with cancer,â the authors wrote. Read More: Mother fears children poisoned by cancer-causing âforever chemicalsâ near factory Read More: NHS trust to review 4,500 more breast cancer cases after failings They said that there are âare no consequencesâ if targets set out in the Nation Cancer Plan are not reached as they called for legal accountability. They wrote that the Health Bill âcontains no statutory duties to improve cancer outcomesâ and said that âimprovement will only occur with a statutory requirement to measure and report meaningful cancer metricsâ. The authors concluded that policy documents such as the National Cancer Plan âcan and are being delayed, diluted, underfunded, or simply not delivered without consequenceâ. They added: âPlans express intent; legislation creates enduring obligations and accountability. England no longer has a cancer plan problem; it has an accountability problem.â Prof Price, lead author of the paper, said: âEnsuring cancer patients get their treatment on time needs to be a priority, and that is why we are calling for accountability to be enshrined in legislation.â Mark Lawler, professor of digital health at Queenâs University Belfast, and senior author on the paper, added: âCurrently there are no consequences if targets are not reached. âThis is why we are calling for legal accountability. It works well in Denmark, which shows the greatest improvement in cancer outcomes in Europe, while the UK flounders. âIt can work here, but only if we have the courage to make this decision to embed a legal right for cancer patients. Itâs the only way we see to avoid an impending cancer epidemic from which we may never recover.â The Department of Health and Social Care has been approached for comment. https://www.dw.com/en/india-sonia-gandhi.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PHo8 Prefer DW on Google Sonia Gandhi has said that her memoir is not a 'political book' but a 'personal' one [FILE: Jun 4, 2024] Image: Sondeep Shankar/Pacific Press/picture alliance Advertisement A memoir by senior Congress leader and former party president Sonia Gandhi went on sale on Tuesday, with its pages offering a rare insight by the private politician into how she came from humble Italian origins and went on to become the matriarch of India's most powerful political dynasty — the Nehru-Gandhi family. The book called "Belonging: A Journey of Love" has been published by HarperCollins India. "Much has been written about my family, but rarely with real insight into who they were, their motivations, their struggles, their very human flaws. I wanted to portray them honestly, as people I knew and loved," 79-year-old Gandhi wrote in The Hindu daily newspaper earlier this week. Who is Sonia Gandhi? Born Sonia Maino in 1946 in a small Italian village near Vicenza, she met Rajiv Gandhi — the grandson of India's first Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru — at a restaurant in the United Kingdom's Cambridge city. The two got married in New Delhi in 1968, when Rajiv's mother and Nehru's daughter Indira Gandhi was serving as India's prime minister. Nearly two decades later, Sonia would find herself holding her bloodied and dying mother-in-law in her arms following a 1984 assassination that saw Indira's bodyguards shoot her to avenge her suppression of an insurgency that culminated in an army assault, called Operation Blue Star, on the holiest Sikh shrine, the Golden Temple. Sonia's husband Rajiv Gandhi, a pilot who was propelled into politics after his mother's death, became India's youngest prime minister at 40 years old. He too was assassinated in a suicide bombing in 1991. Sonia Gandhi later entered politics, going on to become the longest-serving president of the Congress party. India's Congress Party hopes to make comeback To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Sonia Gandhi's book sheds light on India's politically influential Nehru-Gandhi family The Nehru-Gandhi family gave India three prime ministers. In her book Sonia Gandhi talks about her 2004 decision to not take up the top job as prime minister of the world's largest democracy. In an excerpt from her book, published in The Indian Express , Sonia said her children — and now senior Congress leader Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and leader of opposition Rahul Gandhi — had then discussed with her, their mother's possible prime ministership. "One of them asked me straight out whether I would accept the post, just in case our party pulled off a victory. 'Absolutely not' I'd said, almost indignantly,' the excerpt read. "Neither Rahul nor Priyanka felt that I should become prime minister. They'd lived through the trauma of their grandmother's assassination and the brutal murder of their father. In their minds, holding that office was intrinsically linked with heightened danger. They looked relieved and I, too, felt lighter, having said my views out loud on the question for the first time," Sonia writes. Ruling BJP accuses Sonia Gandhi of 'whitewashing' Sonia Gandhi has said that her memoir is not a "political book" but a "personal" one. But with the Tuesday launch, the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) of Prime Minister Narendra Modi attacked the Congress veteran. BJP National spokesperson C R Kesavan said that Sonia Gandhi should have named her book "whitewashing" as he accused the memoir of "sugar coating the historical wrongs perpetrated by the Nehru-Gandhi family." The book has also been released at a time when the Congress party looks to regain ground against the BJP, with Sonia's son Rahul Gandhi rallying India's opposition parties in a series of protests over the last month.
